meta.title: Who really said "There are only four stories: the siege of a city, the return home, the quest, and the suicide of a god"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Paulo Coelho. The four-stories idea is Jorge Luis Borges’s, from his 1972 essay “The Four Cycles”; “suicide of a god” paraphrases his “sacrifice of a god.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There are only four stories: the siege of a city, the return home, the quest, and the suicide of a god'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Coelho — the four-stories idea comes from Jorge Luis Borges’s 1972 essay “Los cuatro ciclos” (“The Four Cycles”).

answer.label: Not Paulo Coelho — actually Jorge Luis Borges
answer.sourceLine: The idea is genuinely Borges’s. In his short essay “Los cuatro ciclos” (“The Four Cycles”), in El oro de los tigres (1972), he names four eternal stories—the siege of a city, the return, the quest, and the sacrifice of a god—concluding, “Four are the stories.” The circulating “suicide of a god” wording is a loose paraphrase (Borges wrote sacrifice), and the line is frequently mis-credited to Paulo Coelho ↗.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: “Los cuatro ciclos” (“The Four Cycles”), in El oro de los tigres
“Suicide of a god” is a paraphrase of Borges’s “the sacrifice of a god”

source.excerpt: Borges reviews four stories: a strong city besieged and defended by brave men (Troy); a return (Ulysses to Ithaca); a search or quest (Jason and the Fleece, the birds seeking the Simurgh, Ahab and the whale); and the sacrifice of a god (Attis, Odin, Christ). He closes: “Four are the stories. During the time left to us we will continue telling them, transformed.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the line to Borges’s essay “Los cuatro ciclos” in El oro de los tigres (Emecé, Buenos Aires, 1972), verified against scans of the original Spanish edition.
Borges lists the four as the siege of a city, the return, the quest, and the sacrifice of a god, ending “Four are the stories… we will continue telling them, transformed ↗.”

Paulo Coelho himself credited Borges—but with a different, incorrect list (“a love story between two people, a love story between three people, the struggle for power and the voyage ↗”), which is neither Borges’s wording nor the version pinned on Coelho online.
source.excerptNote: English rendering per Quote Investigator, from Borges’s Spanish original; the popular “siege / return / quest / suicide of a god” list is a compressed paraphrase of this essay.

author.name: Jorge Luis Borges
author.heading: About Jorge Luis Borges
author.bio: Jorge Luis Borges was an Argentine short-story writer, essayist and poet whose labyrinthine fictions—Ficciones, El Aleph—reshaped 20th-century literature. He was fascinated by recurring archetypes and the idea that literature endlessly retells a handful of stories. His late essay “Los cuatro ciclos” distilled that conviction into the famous claim that there are only four.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: On social media the “four stories” line is routinely pinned on Paulo Coelho, a top magnet for tidy, quotable wisdom. The idea is not his—and even the wording usually quoted is not exactly Borges’s.

items.why: Coelho is widely credited with the “siege / return / quest / suicide of a god” formulation, but it originates in Jorge Luis Borges’s 1972 essay “Los cuatro ciclos,” as documented by Quote Investigator ↗. Coelho did discuss Borges’s “four stories,” but gave a completely different (and inaccurate) list.

Borges wrote of “el sacrificio de un dios”—the sacrifice of a god (Attis, Odin, Christ). “Suicide of a god” is a later, looser English rendering, not Borges’s literal term, per QI’s translation of the essay ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and its four categories are genuinely Borges’s, from “Los cuatro ciclos” in El oro de los tigres (1972) ↗—not Paulo Coelho—and Borges’s own word was “sacrifice,” not “suicide.”

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Borges’s claim is a compact theory of all storytelling: strip away the surface and every tale is one of four archetypes—a city besieged, a homecoming, a quest, or a god who dies. It is catnip for writers and readers because it flatters the sense that literature is a single, endlessly retold myth.

That universality is also why it drifts so easily onto a feel-good name like Coelho’s. The irony is that Coelho did invoke Borges’s “four stories”—but garbled them into a different list, helping seed the confusion.
